Intention: what this notebook is for¶

C's part of the group project is research question 2.2. On a real urban district imported from OpenStreetMap, C sweeps the network density (vehicles in the network ÷ total lane length) at a constant vehicle count, to find the density where network flow peaks (the network critical density), to test whether local jams merge into large congested clusters near it, and to test whether edge betweenness predicts where congestion starts. The district is Bugis–Rochor–Lavender in Singapore; C's task 1 imported its road network from OpenStreetMap and cleaned it. The cars and their destinations are synthetic, so the project overview (team repo Project_Overview_EN.md §8) calls these "synthetic-demand experiments on a real network topology": real traffic data are a reference for where and how much congestion occurs, not a calibration.

Member E makes that reference comparison: where does the simulation jam, and where are real Singapore roads slow? LTA DataMall's Traffic Speed Bands feed supplies the real side, one speed band every 5 min for each LTA road stretch. C's task 2, the subject of this notebook, builds the two things the comparison needs:

  • a lookup that says on which SUMO edge (a road piece of the simulated network) each LTA road stretch lies;
  • a speed history, because LTA serves only the current 5 minutes and keeps no history, so C polls the feed and stores every update.

This notebook rebuilds the lookup from the real LTA feed, shows where matching succeeds and fails and why (§3–§7), tests how much the result depends on the snap radius (§8), compares it with the 2024 sample behind the first prototype (§9), draws a random spot-check sample (§10) and shows the first speed data stored (§11). The section "Using the lookup (for member E)", near the end, explains the tables.

Issues found, and their state on 2026-10-21¶

  1. Arterial coverage is below its target: open. Matcher A places 0.754 of the 1,303 arterial stretches (LTA categories 2 and 3) in the whole network, against a target of 0.85 set before the build (row 6 of the checks table, §4). Inside the study box, major arterials reach 731 of 868 (0.84) and arterials 194 of 306 (0.63). The matching settings (T2-D5) are open.
  2. Very short stretches fail the direction test: open. Inside the study box, neither matcher places 1,091 stretches. The largest single group, 396 (36 %), lie on roads the network has, but the nearest edge points 45–135° away from the stretch's start-to-end heading. Stretches of 5 m or less are placed 46 % of the time, against 72–74 % for stretches longer than 15 m, so a noisy heading on very short stretches is the likely cause (ASSUMED from the length table in §7, not checked stretch by stretch). C recommends testing a different direction test for stretches shorter than about 10 m before widening the radius (T2-D5).
  3. Roads that task 1's cleaning removed: open, belongs to task 1. 278 of the 1,091 (406 in the whole network, margin included) lie on roads that task 1's strong-component pass deleted, for example Republic Avenue and Republic Boulevard, and parts of Queen Street and Fort Canning Road. No matcher setting can recover them. Task 1 has two open items that may restore some roads before the network freeze: a gap fix for 7 missing roads and 7 one-way edges, and a trace of 6.46 lane-km removed more than 600 m inside the box.
  4. Roads the network lacks: open, belongs to task 1. 188 of the 1,091 (232 in the whole network) lie on roads with no SUMO edge of that name, mostly short roads and lanes such as Canning Rise and Coleman Lane.
  5. The lookup is pinned to the network before the signal rebuild: open. The edge IDs still apply, but the pinned sha256 no longer matches, so the lookup must be rebuilt as lookup v1 once T2-D5 is agreed and the network is frozen (T1-D9). Lookup v1 must contain both the links table and the pairs table, because the join from speed bands to SUMO edges needs the pairs' weights.
  6. Only one afternoon of speed data at execution: collection running; hand-over open. The notebook saw 11 polls, from the first complete poll at 14:54 SGT on 2026-10-20 (a one-off test) to 15:40 SGT, and no night. Continuous polling every 5 min has run since 14:58 SGT, nights included; this copy does not show the newer data. The hand-over is issue 9.
  7. The first poll was cut at 100,000 stretches: fixed, one code path left. An old page cap truncated it. The poller now allows 1,000 pages and fails loudly at the cap (2026-10-20 14:58), and the truncated file is excluded (row 9 of the checks table). lta.fetch_all_pages still defaults to 200 pages and truncates silently when called directly; only scripts/lta_poll.py passes the higher cap (open).
  8. No spot-check verdicts yet: optional (T2-D8). The 62-stretch random sample of §10 has no verdicts, so the wrong-road rate of matched stretches is not estimated yet. Road-name agreement (0.94 of matcher A's matches) is the only proxy so far.
  9. Prototype tables and speed history not yet handed to member E: open. The route, format and date are not agreed. The polls take about 309 MB a day and sit in git-ignored data/raw/ on C's machine.

Rationale: the principles behind the design¶

  • Match by geometry and direction, not by name. Road names differ in spelling and abbreviation between LTA and OpenStreetMap, and both directions of a road share one name. Matcher A therefore snaps a stretch's two end points to edges that point the same way and follows the drivable path between them, so the two directions of a road land on different edges (row 3 of the checks table: 0 of 216 twin pairs share an edge). Road-name agreement is recorded as evidence and never used as a filter (0.94 of matcher A's matches agree).
  • Two independent matchers. Matcher B keeps every same-direction edge inside a band reaching 15 m either side of the stretch, and so cross-checks matcher A. A stretch that both place on the same edges, with the same road name, gets confidence = high.
  • A snap radius chosen between 25 m and 30 m. A wider radius places more stretches, but more of them on the wrong road (§8). From 25 m to 30 m, major arterials rise from 0.842 to 0.877, above the 0.85 target, while the share of minor-arterial matches with the same road name drops by about one point (0.913 to 0.904); its fall to 0.816 comes between 30 m and 40 m. Minor arterials, small roads and slip roads keep rising up to 40 m, so they show no plateau. Both 25 m and 30 m are defensible: C recommends 25 m with a 45° heading tolerance, and T2-D5 chooses.
  • Many-to-many, with weights. An LTA stretch can cover several SUMO edges and an edge can carry several stretches, so each stretch–edge pair carries two weights. frac_of_edge is the share of the edge the stretch covers. frac_of_lta differs by matcher: for matcher A it is the share of A's matched path on that edge, so A's rows for a stretch sum to 1; for matcher B it is the overlap divided by the straight stretch length, not normalised. A per-edge speed is the frac_of_edge-weighted mean of its stretches.
  • Poll everything, every 5 minutes, whole days. LTA updates the bands every 5 min and keeps no history. C stores every poll island-wide, so the history does not depend on the district choice, and around the clock, because a stretch's night-time speed is its reference free-flow speed and weekends give a no-commute contrast (T2-D2). The cost is about 309 MB per day.
  • Prototypes cannot leak into results. The valid_for_results flag follows the LTA source label: lta.py (c/city-network, about L359) sets it true only for v4 input whose label lacks "PROTOTYPE". This run's label is v4-links-20261020-PROTOTYPE-T2D5-open, so every row carries valid_for_results = false; C keeps the label until T2-D5 is agreed and the network is frozen. Tables built from the 2024 sample are prototypes too (T2-D3).
  • Bands are not speeds. LTA reports 10 km/h bands. Where a number is needed, this notebook uses the band's midpoint, so differences smaller than one band are not real.

Approach. C built the lookup with the committed script scripts/lta_lookup.py (team c/city-network @ fb45b67) from two inputs: LTA's v4 list of road stretches (143,787 island-wide, taken from the poller's links file) and task 1's network scenarios/city/bugis_all.net.xml as it was before the signal rebuild. Stretches within 50 m of the network's boundary are skipped, which leaves 3,742; 3,368 of them have both end points inside the study box. Both matchers run on every stretch. For each stretch neither matcher places, §3 assigns one cause, in this order: (1) removed by cleaning, when the stretch, matched again on task 1's stage-1 network, lands on an edge the strong-component pass deleted; (2) road missing, when no edge carries its road name; (3) present but unmatched, with the reason read from the nearest edge. The speed data come from the poller's stored files, listed once at the start of the run, so every number refers to the same 11 polls.

Results, and what they mean for each member¶

  • Holds, as a prototype: matcher A places 2,413 of the 3,742 stretches inside the network (0.645). Its matches carry the same road name 0.94 of the time, the two directions of a road never share an edge, and twin stretches sit on the left of each other (81 left, 34 right), as left-hand traffic requires. Re-matching inside the notebook reproduces every stretch's edges.
  • Holds: arterial coverage is 0.754 against the 0.85 target. Inside the box, matcher A places major arterials 0.84, arterials 0.63, minor arterials 0.54 and small roads 0.68 of the time.
  • Holds: of the 1,091 stretches inside the box that neither matcher places, 396 fail the direction test, 278 lie on roads task 1's cleaning removed, 211 have no edge within 25 m, 188 lie on roads the network lacks, 16 have only an opposite-direction edge nearby and 2 fail the detour limit.
  • Holds: 25 m and 30 m are both defensible radii. Major arterials rise from 0.842 at 25 m to 0.877 at 30 m (above the 0.85 target) and 0.895 at 40 m, at about one point of same-name share on minor arterials up to 30 m; minor arterials, small roads and slip roads keep rising up to 40 m.
  • Holds: the 2024 sample gave almost the same overall rate (0.641 against 0.645), but its stretches were much longer (median 77 m against 28 m), so it could not reveal the short-stretch failures.
  • Superseded: the speed figures of §11 show the first 11 polls only. The first complete poll was stored at 14:54 SGT on 2026-10-20, a one-off test; continuous polling every 5 min has run since 14:58 SGT, nights included.
  • Provisional: the whole lookup is a prototype (valid_for_results = false) built on the network before the signal rebuild; lookup v1 follows T2-D5 and the network freeze.

For member E:

  • The section "Using the lookup (for member E)" below gives the tables' columns, three example rows and the join from a speed-band poll to SUMO edges.
  • Unplaced stretches drop out of the join by themselves, because they have no pairs. Report them by cause: inside the study box, 278 lie on roads removed by cleaning, 188 on roads the network lacks and 625 on roads it has; in the whole network, the first two are 406 and 232. The lookup files do not carry this cause: this notebook computes it. Lookup v1 should carry a cause column or ship a LinkID list per cause (C's plan, not yet built).
  • A 30 m snap radius would lift major-arterial coverage from 0.842 to 0.877, above the target, at about one point of same-name share on minor arterials (0.913 to 0.904). The radius is T2-D5, to agree with C.
  • The speed history sits on C's machine (git-ignored data/raw/lta_speedbands_v4/, about 309 MB per day). Handing it and the prototype tables over is open (issue 9), and the group has yet to agree the polling plan (T2-D2).

For member D: a closure or new-link variant has its own network file, and this lookup covers the baseline network only, so a variant needs its own lookup run before any LTA comparison.

For member A: the lookup and poller code (src/traffic_project/lta.py, scripts/lta_lookup.py, scripts/lta_poll.py) is on c/city-network and reaches main through a pull request for member A's review. lta.fetch_all_pages keeps a silent 200-page default (issue 7).

Strong-component pass Task 1's cleaning step: it keeps only roads from which a car can reach every other road and come back, so it deletes one-way pieces the cut left without a way in or out
Matcher A, matcher B A snaps both end points and follows the drivable path between them (the result); B keeps same-direction edges within 15 m either side (the cross-check)
Twin pair The two stretches of a two-way road, one per direction, whose end points are each other's swapped

3. Load the lookup and sort every stretch by result and cause¶

What the lookup is. LTA splits Singapore's roads into short stretches (LTA calls them links), each one direction of travel, with a start point, an end point, a road name and a road category. Every 5 minutes it publishes one speed band per stretch. The lookup says which SUMO edge (road piece of our simulated network) each stretch lies on. Two matchers run on every stretch inside the net. Matcher A snaps the start and the end point to edges within the snap radius (25 m) that point the same way (within 45°) and follows the shortest drivable path between them. Matcher B keeps every same-direction edge that runs inside a 15 m band around the stretch. A is the result and B the cross-check. A stretch is matched by both, by one, or by none.

C built the lookup with the committed script and a sandbox copy of its config, kept in C's git-ignored sandbox/c/notebooks/configs/; the copy has the same matching settings as configs/city/lta_lookup.toml and the real v4 input (one config, one command):

export SUMO_HOME=/usr/share/sumo
python scripts/lta_lookup.py --config sandbox/c/notebooks/configs/lta_lookup_v4.toml   # 3.6 s

The cell below loads its output and gives each unmatched stretch one cause, in this order. (1) Removed by cleaning: matched again against the task 1 stage-1 net (before the strong-component pass), the stretch lands on an edge that pass removed. (2) Road missing from the net: no edge carries the stretch's road name. (3) Present but unmatched: the road is in the net but the matcher found no edge. For (3), it also looks at the nearest edge to the failing end point, ignoring direction, to say why.

In [3]:
CAT_NAME = {1: "1 expressway", 2: "2 major arterial", 3: "3 arterial", 4: "4 minor arterial", 5: "5 small road",
            6: "6 slip road", 8: "8 short tunnel"}            # API guide v6.10 §2.19 (RoadCategory)
links = lta.load_links(POLLDIR / "links.parquet")
lt = pd.read_csv(f"{PRE}_links.csv", dtype={"lta_link_id": str})
pairs = pd.read_csv(f"{PRE}_pairs.csv", dtype={"lta_link_id": str})
CHK = json.loads(Path(f"{PRE}_checks.json").read_text())
MAN = json.loads((OUT / "manifest.json").read_text())
w, s, e, n = BOX
lt["in_box"] = (lt.lta_start_lon.between(w, e) & lt.lta_start_lat.between(s, n) & lt.lta_end_lon.between(w, e)
                & lt.lta_end_lat.between(s, n))
lt["match"] = np.where(lt.a_matched & lt.b_matched, "both", np.where(lt.a_matched | lt.b_matched, "one", "none"))
lt["cat"] = lt.lta_category_code.map(CAT_NAME)

# cause (1): re-match the unmatched stretches on the stage-1 net
un_ids = set(lt.loc[lt.match == "none", "lta_link_id"])
_, s1tab, _ = lta.match_links(RUN1 / "stage1.net.xml", links[links.LinkID.isin(un_ids)], lta.MatchParams(**LCFG["match"]))
KEPT = set((RUN1 / "scc_edges.txt").read_text().split())
s1tab["edges"] = (s1tab.a_edges.fillna("") + " " + s1tab.b_edges.fillna("")).str.split()
removed_ids = set(s1tab.loc[s1tab.edges.apply(lambda es: bool(es) and any(x not in KEPT for x in es)), "lta_link_id"])

# cause (3) detail: nearest passenger edge to the failing end point, any direction
fin, fnet = cm.net_edges(NETF)
def nearest(lon, lat, hdg):
    x, y = fnet.convertLonLat2XY(lon, lat)
    best = None
    for ed, _ in fnet.getNeighboringEdges(x, y, 60.0, includeJunctions=False):
        if not ed.allows("passenger"):
            continue
        off, d = cm.sumolib.geomhelper.polygonOffsetAndDistanceToPoint((x, y), ed.getShape(), perpendicular=False)
        dh = lta.ang_diff(lta.local_heading(ed.getShape(), off), hdg)
        if best is None or d < best[0]:
            best = (d, dh, ed.getName())
    return best or (np.inf, np.nan, "")
def cause(r):
    if r.match != "none":
        return ""
    if r.lta_link_id in removed_ids:
        return "removed by cleaning"
    if r.qa_flag == "absent-from-net":
        return "road missing from the net"
    return "present but unmatched"
def detail(r):
    if r.cause != "present but unmatched":
        return ""
    if "detour" in r.qa_flag:
        return "path between end points too long (detour)"
    end = "end" in r.qa_flag
    d, dh, _ = nearest(r.lta_end_lon if end else r.lta_start_lon, r.lta_end_lat if end else r.lta_start_lat, r.lta_heading_deg)
    if d > LCFG["match"]["radius"]:
        return f"no edge within {LCFG['match']['radius']:.0f} m"
    if dh > 135:
        return "only an opposite-direction edge nearby"
    return "nearby edge points 45-135 deg off"
lt["cause"] = lt.apply(cause, axis=1)
lt["detail"] = lt.apply(detail, axis=1)
print(f"LTA stretches island-wide: {len(links):,}; inside the net (less a {LCFG['match']['margin']:.0f} m margin): {len(lt):,}; "
      f"of these inside the study box: {int(lt.in_box.sum()):,}")
display(pd.crosstab([lt.in_box.map({True: "inside box", False: "margin"}), lt.cat], lt.match, margins=True))

4. Checks¶

Each row is one property the lookup or the stored speed data must have. Rows 3–6 are the four failure checks C set before building the lookup (lta.run_checks, thresholds from the config); their names carry their own numbers, 1–4. In the text, "row n" means the # column of the table. A failing check is shown, not raised, so the figures below can show why.

In [4]:

def by_cat(d):
    g = d.groupby("cat")
    return pd.DataFrame({"total": g.size(), "matched": g.a_matched.sum(),
                         "missing_from_net": g.cause.apply(lambda x: (x == "road missing from the net").sum()),
                         "removed_by_cleaning": g.cause.apply(lambda x: (x == "removed by cleaning").sum()),
                         "present_unmatched": g.cause.apply(lambda x: (x == "present but unmatched").sum()),
                         "b_only": g.apply(lambda x: (x.b_matched & ~x.a_matched).sum(), include_groups=False)})

Update 2026-10-21: the direction test is the largest single cause of failure, not most of it. It accounts for 396 of the 1,091 stretches inside the box that neither matcher places (36 %), and for 396 of the 625 that lie on roads the network has. The other unplaced stretches lie on roads removed by cleaning (278), have no edge within 25 m (211), lie on roads the network lacks (188), face only an opposite-direction edge (16) or fail the detour limit (2).

What to notice: major arterials match best, 731 of 868 stretches (0.84), just under the 0.85 target. Arterials reach only 194 of 306 (0.63), and their failures split between roads removed by cleaning (58) and stretches present but unmatched (43). Minor arterials have the most failures: 331 of 1,065 stretches are present in the net but unmatched. The reason tables show what fails: in 396 of the 625 present-but-unmatched stretches the nearest edge points 45–135° away from the stretch, and in 211 no edge lies within 25 m (8 of those are East Coast Parkway, an expressway the net excludes on purpose, T1-D2). Only 16 face an opposite-direction edge alone, the sign of a net that lacks one direction. Stretches of 5 m or less match only 46 % of the time, against 72–74 % for stretches longer than 15 m: on a stretch that short, the start-to-end heading is unreliable. So the largest single fix belongs in the task 2 matcher's direction test for short stretches, and the cleaning losses belong to task 1. This is VERIFIED for the counts. That short stretches fail because of a noisy heading is ASSUMED from the length table; it has not been checked stretch by stretch.

8. Does the match rate depend on the snap radius? (T2-D5)¶

What to look at: how far each line moves between 10 m and 40 m, and where it flattens. The black vertical line marks the recommended 25 m. Each line is one LTA road category (inside the study box; n in the legend); the y-axis is the share of stretches matched by matcher A. Only the radius changes; bearing 45°, detour 1.5 and the rest stay at the config values.

Update 2026-10-21: this paragraph was rewritten with the exact values of the two tables above. The 2026-10-20 text called 25–30 m the range where coverage is near its plateau, but three categories keep rising up to 40 m, and it said every category loses a lot below 20 m, but small roads lose only 0.06.

What to notice: from 25 m to 30 m the major-arterial rate rises from 0.842 to 0.877, above the 0.85 target, while the share of minor-arterial matches with the same road name drops by about one point (0.913 to 0.904); its fall to 0.816 comes between 30 m and 40 m. From 25 m to 40 m the major-arterial rate reaches 0.895 and the arterial rate rises from 0.634 to 0.663. Minor arterials (0.541 to 0.638), small roads (0.680 to 0.732) and slip roads (0.475 to 0.590) keep rising up to 40 m, so they show no plateau. Below 25 m, down to 10 m, major arterials, arterials, minor arterials and slip roads lose 0.15–0.23 (major arterials 0.612 at 10 m); small roads lose only 0.06. A larger radius buys coverage partly with wrong roads, and it cannot fix the direction-test failures of §7. So 25 m and 30 m are both defensible, and T2-D5 chooses between them. C's provisional recommendation for T2-D5: keep 25 m and the 45° bearing, and test a change to the direction test for stretches shorter than about 10 m before widening the radius. No seed spread applies here: the matcher is deterministic.

The 2024 sample therefore could not show the short-stretch failures of §7. 10. Spot-check sample (CSV with Street View links)¶

The cell below draws up to 10 stretches per road category at random (seed 20261020) from the stretches inside the study box, matched or not, and writes them to task2-spotcheck-sample.csv. Each row has a Street View link at the stretch's midpoint, facing its direction of travel, plus the edges matcher A chose. A reviewer opens a link, checks whether the road in view is the road in sumo_edge_names and whether traffic ahead goes the stretch's way, and fills in your_verdict (correct / wrong / unsure). A random sample, not the worst cases, tells us the error rate.

In [10]:
def bearing(lon1, lat1, lon2, lat2):
    return (math.degrees(math.atan2((lon2 - lon1) * math.cos(math.radians(lat1)), lat2 - lat1)) + 360) % 360
names = dict(zip(fin.id, fin.name))
SPOT = (pd.concat([g.sample(min(10, len(g)), random_state=20261020) for _, g in lt[lt.in_box].groupby("cat")])
        .assign(mid_lat=lambda d: (d.lta_start_lat + d.lta_end_lat) / 2, mid_lon=lambda d: (d.lta_start_lon + d.lta_end_lon) / 2))
SPOT["heading_deg"] = [round(bearing(a, b, c, d)) for a, b, c, d in zip(SPOT.lta_start_lon, SPOT.lta_start_lat, SPOT.lta_end_lon, SPOT.lta_end_lat)]
SPOT["street_view"] = [f"{cm.streetview(la, lo)}&heading={h}&pitch=0&fov=80" for la, lo, h in zip(SPOT.mid_lat, SPOT.mid_lon, SPOT.heading_deg)]
SPOT["osm_map"] = [f"https://www.openstreetmap.org/?mlat={la:.5f}&mlon={lo:.5f}#map=19/{la:.5f}/{lo:.5f}" for la, lo in zip(SPOT.mid_lat, SPOT.mid_lon)]
SPOT["sumo_edge_names"] = SPOT.a_edges.fillna("").str.split().apply(lambda es: "; ".join(sorted({names.get(x, "?") for x in es})))
SPOT["your_verdict"] = ""; SPOT["note"] = ""
cols = ["cat", "lta_link_id", "lta_road_name", "lta_len_m", "heading_deg", "match", "cause", "detail", "a_edges", "sumo_edge_names",
        "a_name_exact", "a_snap_start_m", "a_snap_end_m", "street_view", "osm_map", "your_verdict", "note"]
SPOT[cols].to_csv(NB_OUT / "task2-spotcheck-sample.csv", index=False)
print(f"wrote {len(SPOT)} rows to out/task2-spotcheck-sample.csv; per category:", SPOT.cat.value_counts().sort_index().to_dict())
display(HTML(SPOT[cols[:8]].assign(street_view=[f'<a href="{u}" target="_blank">Street View</a>' for u in SPOT.street_view])
             .to_html(escape=False, index=False)))

11. The speed data collected so far¶

The poller has stored one file per poll since 14:54 SGT on 2026-10-20 (T2-D4), island-wide (T2-D2). LTA reports a speed band, not a speed: band 1 = 0–9 km/h, 2 = 10–19 km/h, … 7 = 60–69 km/h, 8 = 70 km/h or more (API guide v6.10 §2.19). Band 0 carries no range and is treated as "no data". Where a speed is needed, this notebook uses the band's midpoint (4.5, 14.5, … 64.5 km/h) and 75 km/h for band 8 (ASSUMED: band 8 has no upper limit; the feed reports its maximum as 999 km/h).

What to look at: rows that stay dark across many columns, that is, stretches slow in poll after poll. Each row is one LTA stretch matched to the net inside the study box, in categories 2 (major arterial) and 3 (arterial), the main comparison T2-D6 recommends. ART = STR[(STR.match != "none") & STR.in_box & STR.lta_category_code.isin([2, 3])][["link_id", "cat"]]
H = SP[SP.LinkID.isin(ART.link_id)].copy()
H["tod"] = H.t_sgt.dt.floor("5min").dt.strftime("%H:%M")
H["daytype"] = np.where(H.t_sgt.dt.dayofweek >= 5, "weekend", "weekday")
night = H[H.t_sgt.dt.hour.isin([2, 3])].groupby("LinkID").mid_kmh.median()
REL = len(night) > 0
H["val"] = H.mid_kmh / H.LinkID.map(night) if REL else H.mid_kmh

Using the lookup (for member E)¶

Markdown only: no cell computes the rows below; they were copied from the lookup run's files and checked against src/traffic_project/lta.py (c/city-network) on 2026-10-21.

Where the tables are, and their status. The lookup run wrote five files to runs/lta_lookup_v4_bugis/ on C's machine (git-ignored, so not in the team repo): bugis_all_links.csv (3,742 rows, one per LTA stretch inside the network), bugis_all_pairs.csv (5,026 rows, one per stretch, SUMO edge and matcher), bugis_all_missing_roads.csv (LTA road names the network lacks), bugis_all_checks.json (the four failure checks) and manifest.json (config, network and code version). The tables are a prototype. Every row carries valid_for_results = false, because the flag follows the LTA source label: lta.py sets it true only for v4 input whose label lacks "PROTOTYPE", this run's label is v4-links-20261020-PROTOTYPE-T2D5-open, and C keeps that label until T2-D5 is agreed and the network is frozen (T1-D9). The tables were built on the network before the signal rebuild, whose SUMO edge IDs are unchanged.

What lookup v1 must contain. Lookup v1 is planned for member E's data/processed/ folder (team GUIDE.md's repository-layout table, row data/processed/, owner E), after T2-D5 and the freeze. It must contain both tables: the links table, and the pairs table, because the join to SUMO edges needs the pairs' weights. It should also carry each unplaced stretch's cause, as a cause column or a LinkID list per cause (C's plan, not yet built), because the prototype files do not: this notebook computes the cause in §3.

The links table, one row per stretch. The columns a comparison needs:

Column Meaning
lta_link_id LTA's LinkID; read it as text (dtype=str)
lta_road_name, lta_category_code LTA's road name and category code (1–6, 8)
lta_start_lon, lta_start_lat, lta_end_lon, lta_end_lat the stretch's end points, WGS84 degrees
lta_len_m straight start-to-end length in the network's metric x–y (m)
lta_heading_deg start-to-end direction as a math angle in the network's x–y: degrees counter-clockwise from east, −180 to 180. It is not a compass bearing; §10's heading_deg is one (clockwise from north, 0–360)
a_matched, b_matched whether matcher A or matcher B placed the stretch
a_edges, b_edges the SUMO edge IDs each matcher chose, space-separated; empty when it placed nothing
confidence high: A placed it, at least one of A's edges has the exact LTA road name, and B chose the same edges; medium: as high, but B chose other edges or placed nothing; low: placed, but none of A's edges has the exact name, or only B placed it; empty: unplaced
qa_flag empty: placed by matcher A, stretch ≥ 15 m; stub<15m: placed by A, < 15 m; b-only;a-<reason>: placed by matcher B only; in-net-missed;a-<reason>: unplaced, some SUMO edge carries the road's name; absent-from-net: unplaced, no edge carries it. <reason> is why A failed: no-candidate-start or no-candidate-end (no same-direction edge within the radius of that end point), no-path, backward-on-edge, detour (path longer than 1.5 × the stretch + 20 m) or stub<1m
sumo_net, sumo_net_sha256, lta_source, params, valid_for_results which network, LTA input and settings built the row

The pairs table, one row per stretch, SUMO edge and matcher. It carries the weights:

Column Meaning
method A_endpoint_path (matcher A, the result) or B_buffer_overlap (matcher B, the cross-check)
sumo_edge_id, sumo_edge_name, sumo_edge_len_m the SUMO edge, its OpenStreetMap name (empty if unnamed) and its length (m)
overlap_m length of the stretch's match lying on that edge (m)
frac_of_lta matcher A: share of A's matched path on this edge, so A's rows for a stretch sum to 1 (the path runs between the snapped end points and can be shorter than lta_len_m: 69.9 m against 100.6 m for stretch 83172); matcher B: overlap_m ÷ lta_len_m, not normalised
frac_of_edge share of the edge the stretch covers (0–1)
kept matcher B's keep rule (at least half of the stretch or half of the edge); always true for matcher A
name_match exact, partial, none or missing

The pairs table also repeats the stretch's LTA columns and adds QA measures (heading difference, snap distances, Hausdorff distance).

Three example rows, taken from the spot-check stretches of §10; both matchers placed all three. Links table:

lta_link_id Road (category) Length (m) confidence a_edges
13791 Kallang Avenue (4) 22.1 high 633214906
83172 Lavender Street (6, slip road) 100.6 low 538223013#0 651958652
208298 Victoria Street (2) 10.7 high; qa_flag = stub<15m 21665446#0

Matcher A's rows of the pairs table for stretch 83172:

sumo_edge_id Edge length (m) overlap_m frac_of_lta frac_of_edge
538223013#0 (unnamed slip road) 63.2 63.2 0.904 1.000
651958652 (Jalan Besar) 51.5 6.7 0.096 0.130

What to notice: one slip-road stretch covers all of an unnamed edge and clips 6.7 m of Jalan Besar, so its speed speaks for the whole slip road but for only 13 % of the Jalan Besar edge. A's path is 69.9 m long against a straight length of 100.6 m. Its confidence is low because none of A's edges carries the LTA name: one is unnamed and the other is Jalan Besar. The Victoria Street stretch is a 10.7 m stub on a 217.3 m edge (frac_of_edge 0.049): alone, it says little about the whole edge.

Unplaced stretches. A stretch that neither matcher placed has no pairs, so it drops out of the join by itself. Report the dropped stretches by cause: inside the study box, 278 lie on roads removed by cleaning, 188 on roads the network lacks and 625 on roads the network has (§7); in the whole network, the first two are 406 and 232. The lookup files do not carry this cause; this notebook computes it (§3).

Joining a speed-band poll to SUMO edges. The poller stores one parquet file per poll as data/raw/lta_speedbands_v4/speedbands/<YYYYMMDD>/<HHMMSS>.parquet; the folder and file names are Singapore time (SGT), and the poll_time_utc column inside is UTC. Each file has the columns poll_time_utc, LinkID, SpeedBand, MinimumSpeed and MaximumSpeed, one row per stretch island-wide. This gives a speed per SUMO edge for one poll (C ran it on one poll on 2026-10-21: 1,034 edges got a value):

import pandas as pd
from traffic_project import lta

pairs = pd.read_csv("runs/lta_lookup_v4_bugis/bugis_all_pairs.csv", dtype={"lta_link_id": str})
poll = pd.read_parquet(poll_file)                               # one stored poll
poll = poll[poll.SpeedBand.between(1, 8)].copy()                # band 0 = no data
poll["kmh"] = ((poll.MinimumSpeed + poll.MaximumSpeed) / 2).where(poll.SpeedBand < 8, 75.0)
vals = poll.rename(columns={"LinkID": "lta_link_id"})[["lta_link_id", "kmh"]].astype({"lta_link_id": str})
per_edge = lta.aggregate_to_edges(pairs, vals, value_col="kmh")  # matcher A pairs only

lta.aggregate_to_edges keeps matcher A's pairs, weights each stretch's value by frac_of_edge, and returns per SUMO edge the weighted mean, a coverage (the summed frac_of_edge, capped at 1: the share of the edge LTA data cover) and n_links. An edge with low coverage rests on a short stretch and deserves less weight. Band 8 has no upper limit, so the snippet uses 75 km/h for it, as §11 does (ASSUMED).

What to aggregate is a choice: the absolute band midpoint, as above, or each stretch's speed relative to its own night median (02:00–04:00), as §11.4 intends. Over many polls, combine per stretch over time first (for example, the median per time-of-day bin), then aggregate the result to edges. Before joining, check that sumo_net_sha256 in the tables equals the sha256 of the network the simulation ran on, or that the network's edge IDs are unchanged: a SUMO edge ID means something only on the network the lookup was built for.
